newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia turns to NASA astronaut for key Mir repairs.
newsitem.headline: Russia turns to NASA astronaut for key Mir repairs.

text.p: Russian space officials on Wednesday asked American astronaut Michael Foale to make vital repairs to the orbiting Mir station after its commander developed a heart problem.

The decision to sideline Russian commander Vasily Tsibliyev, 43, to an escape vehicle during repairs means Foale will have to study the plan quickly if the current crew is to succeed in restoring Mir's damaged power system next week.
"We understand that the commander cannot do this work because of his medical condition," Mikhail Sinelshchikov, head of the Russian Space Agency's manned flight division, said.

"There are two options. Either it is done by the board engineer and Foale -- that decision will be taken after the results of the first test run, medical tests and a decision by NASA -- or put off to the next crew," he told Reuters.
A three-man Russian-French crew is due to dock with Mir on August 7.

Mission flight director Vladimir Solovyov said a dress rehearsal for the repairs had been set for July 21 after which a final decision on who would do the actual job, tentatively rescheduled for July 24 -- and when -- would be taken with the U.S. space agency NASA.
U.S. officials said the request that the British-born Foale, who has a doctorate in astrophysics, step in was unexpected.

"They caught us I won't say completely by surprise but I guess we really weren't expecting the Russians to come up with this request," said NASA astronaut Leroy Chiao, who is participating in planning at Russian Mission Control outside Moscow.

NASA officials said they had not formally agreed to commit Foale to the operation. But they said he had begun to study the plan that involves donning a spacesuit to reconnect cables to the three undamaged solar panels attached to the Spektr module.
The current crew had been expected to undertake repairs later this week following the June 25 crash between Mir and its unmanned cargo vessel, the worst accident in the station's 11-year history.
But Mission Control doctor Igor Goncharov told Tsibliyev on Tuesday that he needed to take it easy and go on medication after the discovery of a slight irregularity in his heartbeat.
If he undertakes the repair, Foale will man the air lock between the main station and the Spektr module while engineer Alexander Lazutkin partially enters Spektr to lead the repairs.
Russian officials view Tsibliyev, a veteran of a half-year mission in 1993, as more experienced, but said Foale was also up to the task.

"Vasily did EVAs (spacesuit operations) before, so as far as ground controllers...are concerned, it would be easier if Vasily is able to do the job," said deputy flight engineer Sergei Krikalyov. "But I think Mike is able to do this also."

The latest problems have raised doubts over the future of Mir, the world's only space station. But Russian officials were adamant Mir should not be abandoned. "All our experts say it is not rational to stop Mir operations," Solovyov said.
